name: The Weeping European Beech at Morris Arboretum

location.address: Morris Arboretum & Gardens of the University of Pennsylvania, 100 E Northwestern Ave, Philadelphia, PA 19118

verify_notes: Morris Arboretum (the ground's owner) lists it among its Great Trees: native to Europe, planted by the Morrises before 1909 (so at least about 117 years; the planting date is the page's, no upper bound given, age_max is a loose bound, not sourced). Branches droop and root where they touch the ground so new rings of trees form as the original dies; smooth grey elephant-hide bark, red to golden autumn colour, small sap-feeder holes from birds in the trunk. A staff member in the Morris 'hidden gems' post says its trunks are rooted layers of one original mother tree and a dead log in the middle is the original's remains. story:
The tree that started this weeping beech is dead, and it is still lying in the middle. What stands around it is the same tree, rooted again.

Weeping beeches let their branches hang to the ground, and where a branch touches soil it can put down roots and send up a trunk of its own. Over a century at Morris Arboretum that has turned one planting into a ring. A member of the arboretum's staff has written that the trunks you see are rooted layers of a single mother tree, and that the dead log at the centre is what is left of her.

The Morris family planted it before 1909, on the estate that became the arboretum. That makes it at least about 117 years old. How long before 1909 it went in, nobody has said.

Up close the bark is smooth and grey, the elephant hide the arboretum compares it to, and dotted with small holes where sap-feeding birds have drilled for a drink. In autumn the leaves turn from red to gold. The arboretum counts it among its Great Trees.

It grows across from George Rickey's kinetic sculpture Two Lines, which stands on the site of the old Morris mansion near the main entrance. Entry to the arboretum is paid, and the pin marks the arboretum rather than the ring, so head for the sculpture.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a ring of weeping beech trunks around a dead central log. It stands across from George Rickey's kinetic sculpture Two Lines, near the main entrance.

best_time.label: October and November, when the hanging leaves turn from red to gold
